planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring just as new growth emerges, or immediately after flowering.

directions: An old Japanese selection of the youngianum group bearing nodding, pale pink flowers in loose sprays above small heart-shaped leaflets in early to mid spring. The deciduous foliage is finer-textured than larger-flowered epimediums, emerging bronze-tinted before turning soft green. Forms a tidy, slow-spreading clump useful as groundcover in dry shade once established beneath trees.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring before new growth hardens off, replanting promptly to avoid root desiccation.

directions: An English-bred barrenwort hybrid producing deep maroon-red flowers with slender spurs held above bronze-flushed young foliage in spring. The leaves mature to glossy deep green, giving strong color contrast against the bold blooms. Forms a slowly expanding semi-evergreen clump that performs well in humus-rich woodland shade.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in early spring; established clumps tolerate root disturbance poorly so handle rhizomes gently.

directions: An older selection within the versicolor hybrid group, carrying soft yellow flowers flushed with coppery red in mid-spring above foliage that emerges bronze-red before settling to green. The semi-evergreen leaves offer useful winter structure in milder zones. A reliable, slowly spreading groundcover for dry shade beneath deciduous trees.

planting.note: Divide and reset offset rosettes in spring into humus-rich, consistently moist shaded soil.

directions: Forms neat evergreen rosettes of rounded, scalloped, softly hairy leaves, from which wiry stems carry airy sprays of small starry white flowers in late spring. This European woodland species is one of the parents of the familiar London pride saxifrage and shares its ease of culture in cool, shaded sites. Makes a tidy edging or small-scale groundcover where summers stay humid and shaded.

planting.note: Separate rosette offsets in spring and reset into well-drained, humus-rich shaded soil.

directions: Produces rosettes of long-stalked, spoon-shaped evergreen leaves with toothed margins, topped by airy panicles of small white flowers often speckled with red in late spring. Native to woodland banks and rock crevices in Ireland and the Iberian Peninsula, it is another of the parent species behind the classic London pride hybrid. Tolerates deep shade and competes well at the base of trees and shrubs.

planting.note: Divide loose rosette clumps in spring and site in shaded, humus-rich crevices or banks.

directions: A Pyrenean woodland saxifrage forming loose rosettes of toothed, slightly sticky-hairy leaves, with slender stems carrying small white flowers frequently spotted red or pink from late spring into summer. It prefers shaded, humus-rich crevices and streamside banks and is markedly more shade-tolerant than many rockery saxifrages. Less commonly grown than its London pride relatives but just as useful in deep woodland shade.

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall to mimic natural self-sowing; seedlings overwinter and flower the following spring.

directions: A trailing, short-lived species with small ivy-like, scalloped leaves and cheerful little yellow flowers held just above the foliage mat from late winter through spring. It behaves as a self-sowing annual or short-lived perennial in moist, shaded niches such as damp walls, pavement cracks, and streambank shade. Dies back in summer heat but reliably reappears from seed the following cool season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for cold stratification; plants emerge in early spring and flower before summer dormancy.

directions: Produces loose racemes of lavender to purple-pink tubular flowers held above ferny, deeply cut foliage in mid to late spring. A woodland species native to Japan and Korea, it behaves as a short-lived biennial and self-sows readily in moist, humus-rich shaded soil. Site with care, as it can spread assertively into favorable woodland conditions.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Transplant dormant tubers or divisions in early spring into humus-rich, well-drained shaded soil.

directions: Bears clusters of clear blue to violet-blue tubular flowers above finely divided, blue-green ferny foliage in early spring. This tuberous woodland species, native from Korea through northeastern China and the Russian Far East, is valued by collectors for flower color that rivals the more widely grown Corydalis flexuosa. Prefers humus-rich, well-drained shade and goes summer-dormant once foliage yellows.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall; seedlings establish over winter and bloom the following spring before summer die-back.

directions: A slender East Asian woodland annual closely related to Corydalis incisa, bearing short racemes of pale yellow tubular flowers above delicate, finely cut foliage from spring into early summer. It self-sows readily in moist, shaded leaf litter and is grown mainly by woodland garden enthusiasts as a companion to its purple-flowered relative. Foliage and flowering fade with summer heat, with new seedlings appearing the following cool season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring before shoots emerge, keeping several nodes per division.

directions: An Asian Solomon's seal species producing gracefully arching stems lined with paired, pendent, small whitish-green bell flowers in late spring, followed by dark berries in fall. Native to Chinese woodlands, it is grown mainly by specialist collectors and forms slowly spreading rhizomatous clumps. Shares the general woodland garden needs of the more familiar Polygonatum odoratum, thriving in humus-rich, consistently moist shade.

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in early spring, replanting promptly so roots do not dry out.

directions: A lesser-known Chinese Solomon's seal species with slender arching stems and small tubular greenish-white flowers paired along the leaf axils in late spring. It occurs in woodland habitats of western China and is grown in specialist collections more for botanical interest than wide availability. Shares the general cultural needs of other woodland Polygonatum species, preferring humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained shade.
